newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE-Turkish Cypriot poet looks for unity on island.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Turkish Cypriot poet looks for unity on island.

text.p: The poetry of Nese Yasin is full of longing for a life she barely knew before violence between Turkish and Greek Cypriots ripped her childhood apart and forced her family to flee to safer ground.

"They say a person should/ love their homeland/ that's also what/ my father often says/ My homeland/ has been divided in two/ which of the two pieces/ should I love," the Turkish Cypriot writes in the poem "Which Half".

Her slightly bitter words of love and loss reflect the other side of the 23-year-old conflict marked by the diatribes of politicians, the rumblings of militaries and the fluctuations of international interest in the small Mediterranean island.

"I always felt the division very deeply," says the poet, a small woman with long black hair whose eyes grow wide when she recalls the village her family lived in until threats from Greek Cypriots drove them out -- back when Cyprus was still united.

Now Yasin lives in north Nicosia in the breakaway Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, recognised only by Turkey and propped up by 30,000 Turkish troops. But her poetry tries to look over the barbed wire cluttering the U.N.-patrolled no-man's-land that divides the island.

"I have always been writing poetry, and I always had a longing to see the other side and to express this longing," she told Reuters recently during a visit to south Nicosia in Cyprus, the internationally recognised state trying to reclaim the northern third of the island, lost in 1974 when Turkish forces invaded.
BETWEEN DREAMS AND REALITY

Yasin's poetry, with its memories of the "other side", has gained ardent followers in the south where the government wants to promote the idea that the two communities can live together -- as they were supposed to in 1960 when the island got independence from Britain.

One of her poems has been set to music by the popular Greek Cypriot composer Marios Tokas and during her visits to the southern side of the island her poetry readings are crowded and local journalists bombard her with interview requests.
For many Greek Cypriots, it is a rare chance to meet a Turkish Cypriot. Restrictions on movement across the buffer zone keep contact to a minimum.

For Yasin to travel the few kilometres from her flat in the north to her friends in the south, she flies to Istanbul, Athens and then south Cyprus, a whole-day trip that would take 10 minutes if she could just walk across the Green Line splitting Nicosia.

"People recognise her everywhere, even in restaurants they jump up to kiss her," said Marios Michaelides, a Greek Cypriot involved in a U.S.-backed programme that sponsors meetings in the buffer zone between Turkish and Greek Cypriots.

Yasin was just four years old when the intercommunal violence broke out in 1963, sparked by Greek Cypriot attempts to change the constitution that had sought to balance power between the two populations.
Like thousands of other Turkish Cypriots, Yasin's family fled from their village, which was in the south, to a Turkish Cypriot-controlled enclave elsewhere on the island.
Meanwhile, the United Nations sent in peacekeeping troops and in cities such as the capital Nicosia, armed Greek and Turkish Cypriots patrolled their respective neighbourhoods.

When tensions eased in 1967, families like the Yasins started visiting their old homes, where they picked fruit in the garden, exchanged talk with their former Greek Cypriot neighbours and looked at their often looted homes.
But in 1974, even this uneasy camaraderie was shattered.

A band of Greek Cypriots bent on uniting the island with Greece -- another reason for the violence in the 1960s -- staged a coup backed by the military regime then in Athens. Within days, Turkish troops invaded -- and have yet to leave.

Turkey said it came in to protect Turkish Cypriots from the Greek-backed coup. Greek Cypriots say Ankara wanted an excuse to expand. Whatever the truth, the division between the two communities was completed.
"After 1974, we lost half the island," says Yasin, whose poetry has been attacked by Turkish Cypriot nationalists critical of her longing for a united island.

Negotiations to unite the two communities started even before the 1974 invasion and have not gained much in the intervening years. Each side accuses the other of scuttling talks whenever a deal looks near.
The goal is a bi-zonal, bi-communal, federated state, but what that actually means has yet to be agreed upon.
PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH

Some Greek Cypriot analysts say the recently announced decision by Cyprus to buy S-300 anti-aircraft missiles from Russia was born out of frustration at the slow -- some would say nonexistent -- pace of negotiations.
According to this scenario, Cyprus wanted to provoke Turkey into threatening military action -- as in fact happened -- to spur international mediators towards reaching a solution.

When a U.S. envoy rushed to the island in mid-January to calm tensions, Cypriot officials said the missiles would take at least 16 months to arrive. But they implied that if concrete steps to a solution were made in the interim period, the missile deal would be cancelled.

For Yasin, born in the south, raised in the north, a citizen of both the legitimate Republic of Cyprus and the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state, the diplomatic tension just underscores the tragedy of the tale.
"The people in power (on both sides) cannot solve this problem because the way they think does not let them find a solution," she says.
"They want to find a solution for their own community, but they should be looking at both communities."
